citation.sourceDocument: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 (2026 inflation adjustments, reflecting the One Big Beautiful Bill Act)
citation.sourceNote: The seven ordinary-income rates (10/12/22/24/32/35/37%) and their inflation-adjusted thresholds are transcribed from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32, the annual inflation adjustments for taxable years beginning in 2026, reflecting the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Tables 1-4 of §2.01 give the per-status schedules and §2.14 gives the standard deduction: $32,200 married filing jointly and surviving spouse, $24,150 head of household, $16,100 single and married filing separately. Head of household is NOT a scaled version of single: its 12% and 22% bands open at $17,700 and $67,450 rather than $12,400 and $50,400, its 24% band shares single's $105,700, and then the two diverge again — 32% at $201,750 for head of household against $201,775 for single, and 35% at $256,200 against $256,225. Those last two are $25 apart, which is exactly the kind of near-identical pair that gets transcribed as a copy of its neighbour; each is checked against the Revenue Procedure's own '$X plus Y% of the excess' base amount, which reconciles only for the right threshold (head of household $39,207 = 16,155 + 24%·(201,750 − 105,700); single $41,024 = 17,966 + 24%·(201,775 − 105,700)). Omitted at launch fidelity, because the engine models a wage earner taking the standard deduction with no dependents: the additional standard deduction for age 65 or blindness ($1,650, or $2,050 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse), the capped dependent standard deduction, the §199A qualified business income deduction, the alternative minimum tax (which the AMT screener tile covers separately), and every credit. Itemized deductions are modeled separately by the take-home tile's 'big four'. Verified line by line against Rev. Proc. 2025-32 on 2026-08-29.
